speechtext:
leading up to international wars. Instead of trying to blame tariffs for our troubles, we should first of all remove the cause of tariffs. In other words, we should endeavour to raise the purchasing power of the people up to the level where they would be able to buy the total production of the nation or the production of other nations for which their own can be exchanged.
To sum up briefly, if we want to sell abroad we must be prepared to buy from abroad, and if we want to buy from abroad we must be prepared to place money in the hands of the people so that they may be in a position to buy the goods that are brought into the country; otherwise, naturally, the importers will stop bringing in goods. For that reason I deplore the attitude of certain officials in this country in issuing a pamphlet called "International Exchange Union". If these proposals were put into operation the result would be that a great deal of our production would be exchanged for foreign securities instead of for goods. It might not be so in the immediate period after the war; but after a few months, as soon as certain foreign nations have exhausted their quota of international currency, they will be placed in the position of having to pay us in gold or exchange foreign securities for the goods we ship to them. And of course that situation is bound to be resented by all the nations that do not produce gold, and is bound to cause international friction.
I want to touch briefly upon a number of proposals in the speech from the throne which apparently are aimed at raising the purchasing power of the people. First of all, take the question of housing. This statement appears in the speech:
_ A measure to amend and supplement existing housing legislation will be introduced.
It is often suggested that the reason why we have been able to have the type of war effort we have had is that we have had an incentive, the incentive to win the war. In my opinion, after the war a Very good incentive to encourage the people to work for an all-out peace effort would be the objective of a decent home for every family in the country, especially having regard to the returned man. Such a programme would provide a great deal of employment, and the money paid out in the building of houses would help to stimulate the demand for consumer goods.
In the past the type of housing legislation we have had has helped people only in what might be called the middle income brackets. In the future we must have legislation that 
will make it possible for those in the low income brackets to acquire houses. That has not been possible heretofore. If we had legislation of that kind it would mean that money would have to be made available at an extremely low rate of interest. These loans will have to extend over a long period of time and be repaid at a rate not faster than the depreciation of the houses which those people have bought. National housing should be made a national scheme, financed by national money, at a rate of interest at cost of handling accounts, which might be one or two per cent. To talk of a housing scheme for people in the low income brackets and then to charge 5 or 6^ per cent interest is idle; it means that the scheme cannot be carried out effectively.
I welcome the proposal for a floor under agricultural prices, but whether or not that measure will be effective depends entirely upon the level at which the floor is placed. It should be placed closely under what we might call parity prices for agriculture; and when I say parity prices I do not mean the prices based on levels of 1914, or the prices of 1926 or 1929. I mean the level that will assure to farmers their fair share of the national income. And what is that level? According to figures placed before the reconstruction committee by Mr. D. G. MacKenzie, we find that from 1915 to 1919 farmers representing one-third of the population received one-third of the national income. Undoubtedly that was a time when the farmers were receiving parity prices. From 1926 to 1929, however, the farmers received only one-sixth of the national income and from 1930 to 1940 only one-tenth. So, when we advocate parity prices, I think we should have in mind prices which will guarantee the farmers their fair share of the national income; and the only period when that has ever happened was the period from 1915 to 1919.
I am not impressed with the reference to a national scheme of contributory old age pensions on a more generous basis than that at present in operation. What we need to-day is more generous provision for non-contributory pensioners. The people who are in a position to contribute to an old age pension plan are, generally speaking, in a position to buy government annuities. What we want is to take care of those aged individuals who are not in the fortunate position of being able to contribute to any scheme. Certainly there can be no justification for the old age pensioners of to-day or of the future having to accept the very low income that they receive at the present time. We have been told, of course, that if we tried to increase the amount of the old age pension there would be difficulty with some

The Address-Mr. Quelch
of the provinces. That difficulty will exist only as long as we make the provinces contribute to the cost of old age pensions. I should like to see old age pensions paid purely on a national basis, financed by the national government. I do not think any province would object to the old age pension being increased provided the federal government paid the total cost, and in that case there would be no reason why the old age pension could not be increased to $40 per person or $80 for a man and wife, which would give them an income of approximately $1,000 a year.
I very much welcome the government's proposal to pay family allowances. This is a step in the direction we have been advocating for a number of years. We first began to advocate something of this kind in this house in 1936; and I think most hon. members will recall how the suggestion that money should be paid directly to individuals outside the industrial system was scoffed at in this house. We were continually told that we were advocating something for nothing. However, apparently the government now see the light and are proposing to issue money directly to consumers instead of having it paid out through industry.
Since the declaration of war the government have had to travel quite a long way in the direction we have been advocating here since 1936. For instance, in the years when we had many unemployed we urged upon the government the necessity of expanding the amount of money in circulation in order to provide employment. Hon. members who were here at that time will remember how the Minister of Finance of that day would become almost hysterical every time that suggestion was made, and would accuse us of advocating inflation. Well, what has happened since the war? When it became necessary to expand production in this country we did not hesitate to increase the amount of money in circulation, so that to-day we find there is over a billion and a quarter dollars more in circulation than was the case at the beginning of the war, in currency and deposits. Another proposal we made back in 1935 was that a discount should be paid on prices, subsidized by the federal government, to make it possible for industry to sell at less than the cost of production, thereby increasing the purchasing power of the people without any danger of inflation. In those days the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) did not hesitate to ridicule that suggestion. I remember how he claimed that this would cause inflation; yet what have we to-day? We are paying millions of dollars in subsidies to industry to make it possible for
them to sell at less than the cost of production, thereby maintaining the price ceiling; and the minister himself in this house called it a form of insurance against inflation. Back in 1937 it was called inflation; to-day it is insurance against inflation.
Those are a few of the measures we advocated back in 1936 that the government have bad to adopt, though at the time we were ridiculed for having suggested them. Unfortunately, however, the most essential step which must be taken, and which has not been taken up to the present time, is the issue of national money so that national projects can be financed without increasing the interestbearing debt of this country. Until such time as this measure has been taken the government will always be in the difficult position of having either to curtail its expenditures or steadily to expand the national debt.
I should like to make a few brief observations with regard to the amendments now before the house. The amendment offered by the Conservatives contains nothing at which one could take offence, that is anyone sitting on this side of the house. It just refers to the fact that the government has failed to do this and that, and I think we all agree that the government has failed to do these things. Therefore we will support the amendment. .The amendment offered by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation reads:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that in the opinion of this house Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose the fundamental social changes and economic planning which alone can hasten the winning of the war and make possible the establishment of a post-war Canada capable of providing full employment and complete social security.
I think most people, if they are frank, will admit the truth of that statement. If I had been drafting that motion I would have added the words, "with the greatest possible degree of individual freedom", because none of us likes to have regimentation of the individual, and if those words were added it would be made clear that this is not intended by the motion. In drawing up plans for the future we should do everything in our power to avoid bureaucratic controls and regimentation of the people. During this war planning has been absolutely essential; we never could have had a total war effort without planning, and I am satisfied that we shall never have a total peace effort without planning, particularly in the transition period between war and peace and especially in regard to finance. Therefore our group will also support the amendment offered by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.
The Address-Mr. Quelch

I wish now to deal with one of our major responsibilities of to-day; that is, the question of rehabilitating the men of the armed forces. I recall the promises which were made during the last war; I think all hon. members who served in the armed- forces at that time will recall that the men were promised that after they were demobilized they would be guaranteed jobs and their dependents would be looked after. I think most hon. members will agree that we failed miserably to fulfil these promises, and I think we also agree that this must never be allowed to happen again. I was very much interested in an article which appeared in the February issue of the American -magazine entitled "Canada Cares for its Heroes" written by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). The hon. member for Rosthern referred to this article, which is an exceedingly glowing account not only of what Canada is doing but of wrhat Canada will do for her soldiers in the future. This, however, is what puzzles me. If that is a correct statement, why should there be such widespread discontent throughout the country among the returned men and the various returned men's organizations? I think when the minister wrote that article he painted a picture of what he would like to see rather .than a picture of what actually exists, though I am not for one moment suggesting that the minister was not sincere when -he wrote the article. I do not believe there is an hon. member more anxious to see the returned men get a square deal than is the Minister of Pensions and National Health, but of course he has great obstacles to overcome and his word does not necessarily prevail in the cabinet or wherever these things are finally decided.
I shall deal with some of the main causes for the discontent which exists to-day. Just before coming to Ottawa I stayed in Edmonton for a few days and had communication with the Edmonton branch of the Canadian Legion. I found there a tremendous amount of indignation owing to the fact that the men being returned from overseas in a wounded condition were being discharged while still in hospital receiving treatment. One of the cases which received a great deal of publicity was that of Captain Gilchrist. He was seriously wounded overseas and was returned to Canada, but while still in hospital with his leg in a cast he was discharged from the army. His pay was reduced from that of a captain to $44 a month. There was a deduction of $30 a month for hospitalization, so that he received a net income of $14 a month. This man was contributing to the keep of his mother and father, and his case received a great amount of publi-

city. It made returned men in that city simply wild to realize that that is the way men who had been wounded overseas are being treated.
I was pleased when the order in council was brought down in the house to correct this situation, and I trust its operation- will be made retroactive. But I cannot understand why a situation like that was permitted to exist for such a long time. The fact is that it existed for many months, and caused a tremendous amount of indignation in the ranks of the armed forces. Even though we have now changed the situation, that resentment will continue, because the men will have lost confidence in the department and the government and, I think, rightly so.
There appears to be a great deal of carelessness in the way in which men are handled after they are discharged from hospital. While I was in Edmonton I was asked to go out with members of the legion to inspect a certain case. This man had been discharged from the hospital about five days before I made my visit. He was living with his mother at the edge of the city, in one room. There was no furniture in that room, with the exception of a bed. He had not received any clothing allowance or any demobilization pay. The Red Cross later provided him with some clothes. This man had seen service in Sicily and had been severely wounded. He had lost his speech, to the point where he could only say, "Yah". He was not able to use the fingers of his right hand. His right arm and leg w.ere partly paralyzed. In short, he just did not know what it was all about.
The legion had approached certain officials with the idea of having the man- transferred to a convalescent home or a reconditioning centre. They were informed there was no such establishment in Edmonton. But this is what angered the legion representatives: It is a fact that the provincial government of Alberta had offered to the federal government the use of Government House as a convalescent home for soldiers. In the past the provincial government had been receiving from the United States authorities $2,000 a month for the use of that building. The time arrived when the United States tenants stopped using the building, and when that time arrived the use of it was offered to the federal government free of charge, as a convalescent home for the duration of the war and for six months thereafter. That offer was turned down.
But when these men are discharged and the legion asks that they be put into a convalescent home they are told that no such accommodation is available. I understand, however, that reconditioning centres are being

The Address-Mr. Quelch
built for future use at certain points in the Dominion. Action is now being taken, I understand, to send the man in question to Christie street hospital, Toronto, for treatment. But the mere fact that that situation was allowed to exist, a condition which permitted the sending of a man to a house in such poverty-stricken circumstances, arouses the ire of our people. I believe if the man in question had been left there for any length of time he would have become a mental case.
In his article in the American magazine the Minister of Pensions and National Health states, in effect, that the officials of his department will lean over backwards to do justice to the returned men. I believe that is true of the minister, and I do not doubt it is true of the deputy minister. Unfortunately, however, there are many officials across Canada who are either careless or callous, and I think disciplinary action should be taken where the men in charge allow conditions such as I have described to exist. We must assure ourselves that such things will not occur again.
Then, ever since the beginning of the war there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction over the fact that soldiers boarded A1 upon enlistment are refused pension on the ground that their disabilities are of pre-enlistment origin. We have been told in the house that upon enlistment recruits are given a very thorough medical examination. It seems to me therefore that when these men are discharged on account of a disability they should be awarded a pension until their disability is cured, and pension should not be denied them upon the ground of pre-enlistment origin.
Further, I do not like the manner in which some of the men are treated when the medical authorities are trying to find out whether or not the disability was of pre-enlistment origin. It amounts almost to a third degree, and is no credit to the department which allows that kind of thing to take place. I shall not take the time of the house to describe the procedure by which some of these admissions are obtained. I know, however, that very often a medical officer will get into conversation with a soldier, the soldier having no idea that his evidence is being taken down. Then, probably some time later, he may be confronted with the statement he is supposed to have made, in which he has admitted that at some time or another he suffered some slight accident, and that therefore his pension must be refused on the grounds of a disability of preenlistment origin.
The other day I discussed this general situation with a naval officer. He said to me, "The
government is like a lawyer with a bad case, because it tries to settle for the smallest possible amount." That certainly does seem to me to be the general impression throughout Canada. There are -many cases where the applicants would appear to be eligible for certain payments, and yet because of some technical point such payments are refused.
In 1940 I sat on a subcommittee of the pensions committee, dealing with mental cases. That committee recommended that the section debarring a soldier from pension, when disability was of congenital origin, should be deleted. It was my understanding that the clause had been deleted, but I am not now certain whether that is so. Judging from the actions of various medical boards throughout the country one would think that the section is still operative.
Another injustice-and in my opinion a glaring one-is that men who have served overseas for a number of years and who are then returned. to Canada and allowed a discharge on compassionate grounds, are refused any rehabilitation grants. Only this morning I received a letter from the Canadian Legion at Edmonton referring to several such cases. Two of the men to which reference was made in the letter had been enlisted, one for three years and the other for four. Upon returning to Canada they had little or nothing to do, so they asked for their discharge. They were refused any rehabilitation grant, including that of clothing and one month's pay. This is what the legion has to say in the matter:
I think this is one of 'the grievances that certainly should be rectified, as men who have been overseas and are returned to this country certainly get fed up hanging around not doing anything, and they naturally, after a time, make application for discharge which is inevitably granted.
In my opinion any man who has served overseas, no matter for how short a time, and is discharged on compassionate grounds, should be eligible for rehabilitation grants. In so far as those men who have served only in Canada are concerned, it is my opinion that each case would have to be dealt with on its merits. But a man who has had long service, even though he has not been outside Canada, should be eligible for grants On the other hand, if his service has been short, or if he has been in some building rvhere he expects to sit for the duration, such as the Jackson building, it might be a different state of affairs.
I might add that the postscript to the letter is in these words:
I am very pleased to let you know that I have been successful in having Jossul's rehabilitation granted so maybe the others will come through.
I am glad to hear that because that may mean that a new policy has been put into effect
The Address-Mr. Quelch

with regard to t'he granting of rehabilitation rights to these men who get discharged on compassionate grounds.

I am not blaming the minister of pensions by any means for all these injustices. As I have pointed out already, I do not believe that there is any man in this house who is more sincere in his desire to see that these men get a square deal. However, the minister does not have the final say in these matters; he can only recommend, and apparently in the past his recommendations have not received the kind of treatment they should have received.
Another matter which has caused a great deal of dissatisfaction is the fact that men receive only one month's pay and allowance upon discharge. I notice from the speech from the throne that gratuities are to be given. We cannot criticize or commend this proposal until (ve know at just what level these gratuities are to be set. In my opinion when a man returns from overseas he should immediately be given one month's leave with full pay. During that time he could get into touch with his relatives and make plans for the future. Then, when he is discharged he should receive a substantial gratuity based upon his length of service. The Edmonton Legion passed a resolution asking that a man coming back from overseas receive one day's pay for each day's service. I do not think that is asking too much.

The clothing allowance which was given in the past was totally inadequate. This has been increased to $65, but I wonder how many members of parliament would like to buy a complete outfit of clothing for $65. By the time you bought a suit and overcoat you would have exhausted your funds, and you would still need a hat, boots, underwear, et cetera.

speechtext:
Somebody says "braces". They probably would before they got a job. Many soldiers' dependents are suffering injustices. I know this does not come under the minister of pensions, but I have taken up a number of these cases with the dependents' allowance board. I am frank to admit that I have not had much success. There is a practice of stopping a dependents' allowance when a man is absent without leave for a certain length of time. He may be absent without leave for twenty-one days before the dependents' allowance is stopped'-if he is overseas the time limit is three months-but after that time the government jumps to the conclusion that the man is a deserter. We know there are many cases where such men have been blown to pieces in air raids, and instead of the wife continuing to get compensation, she is told that her husband is a deserter and her allowance is cut off. I do not think the dependents' allowance should be cut off until there is positive proof that a man has deserted. Just as long as there is any possibility that he may have been killed, the dependents' allowance should be paid in full.
When a man is finally apprehended and sentenced, we will say, to two years in the army prison his dependents' allowance is paid for six-months, after which time it is stopped. I contend that as long as the army has the man's body they should continue to pay an allowance to his wife and dependents. Why should they take it out of the dependents? We have in this country many wives and children on relief because soldiers are serving sentences in army prison camps. Just as long as the army has the bodies of those men under control they can get a certain amount of work out of them and the dependents' allowances should be paid. They could be charged up against the man who would work it out. I think most people will agree with the justice of this claim. Why should the wife and children be penalized just because a man, perhaps as a result of war service, has developed some kind of mental quirk and refuses to assume his responsibilities. The man cannot always be blamed. Sometimes desertion is a result of mental trouble resulting from the strain of service.

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough West)
Another grievance is that deductions from dependents' allowances are made when the dependent receives hospitalization. There are a number of wives of soldiers in Alberta who are obtaining treatment in the sanitarium for tuberculosis. This treatment is absolutely free in Alberta. Anyone in the province may obtain, free treatment. Yet the dependents' allowance board deducts $20 a month from the allowance of these women and then pays it to the provincial institution as a maintenance cost-. Since this treatment is free in Alberta the province does not want to charge for the maintenance of these women, the provincial government has offered to pay this money over to the dependents, but the dependents' allowance board has ruled that if the provincial government pays this S20 to the dependents, the board will have to make a further deduction. I have taken this matter up with the dependents' allowance board and they tell me that they cannot do anything because they are governed by the departmental regulations. Those regulations are man-made and there is nothing to prevent their being changed. It is high time they were changed. Here we have a most undesirable situation where a civilian can obtain free hospitalization and yet the dependent of a soldier is charged.
In closing, I should like to make a recommendation to the minister. He knows, as we all do, that there is a great deal of criticism of certain of the measures which come under his department and under the dependents' allowance board. I urge that a committee be set up to deal with soldiers' affairs and that the terms of reference should be sufficiently wide to permit it to deal with pensions, dependents' allowances and the reestablishment of the returned soldier.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Queloh) for referring to the wives and families of soldiers who may be A.W.O.L. overseas. I know of a number of cases where wives and children have suffered all kinds of distress because the government just like the cut of a knife has taken away their living. The children's aid society have had to take over in many cases.
I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for referring to old age pensions. He has suggested that the old age pension should be $40 a month. If you look in Hansard for 1940 I believe you will find that I suggested, not only that it be $40 but that the age limit be reduced to sixty years. The old age pension should be given to those people who are in need, not as a charity but as their rightful due.
The speech from the throne this year was a speech that left the people of Canada speechless. When the people read that speech and found out what wras promised-I say promised -by this government they said, I have had them say to me, why, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has promised everything except the kitchen sink. I believe that is right; he has promised everything. I know that the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker), in seconding the motion for the address, certainly hit the nail on the head when he said, as reported at page 16 of Hansard of January 28:
In his book, "Industry and Humanity", written twenty-five years ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) set out certain ideals which we shall seek to attain in regard to better social security. It is not often that a young man who dreams of a programme for the betterment of his country is given a chance twenty-five years later, as prime minister of his country, to begin to carry out in such large measure as is proposed in the speech from the throne that programme.

speechtext: I think every person in Canada will agree with me that the Prime Minister is still dreaming, as the hon. member has just said. Why should the Prime Minister have waited twenty-five years to do these things? He has been in and out of office for practically that length of time-

speechtext:
He is still dreaming and that is what the people believe. The Prime Minister said that we would not have an election this year, but the speech from the throne certainly looks as though the Prime Minister were preparing for an election very soon. It looks as though he had been holding this dream in reserve for twenty-five years, so that he would have something up his sleeve, an ace in the hole, as it is often called, to save him at some future time, because it is only by a miracle that the present government can be saved from defeat at the polls at the next election.
I do not believe that the present government could possibly carry out the programme set forth in the speech from the throne, because a programme of that kind needs to be carried out on sound business principles in order to make it stay with us-not for a year or two, because if we are to have social security of the kind that is set forth in the speech from the throne we do not want it for just a short time but until such a time as a better programme can be found. That is
158	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough West)
why I say that the present government cannot give us the utopia that is set forth in the speech from the throne.
I have often urged in this house and on platforms throughout the country that we should have a better social security set-up in regard to health, particularly, in Canada. But so far as I can see, the speech from the throne does not mention hospitalization at all, and hospitalization is one of the greatest needs, if not the greatest need of the country to-day. Not only the working man and the farmer but you and I, Mr. Speaker, are in fear of having to go to the hospital or have some member of our families requiring hospitalization, and we all know that hospitalization drains one's resources almost to the limit. In the case of the working man and the farmer it would certainly do that. But we have another fear, namely that if by chance we or some member of our family had to go to hospital there would not be a room in any hospital to accommodate the patient. That is the case to-day. Hospitalization should have been one of the subjects dealt with in the speech from the throne. I believe that in any post-war programme hospitalization should have priority. I believe that this government should at once announce to the different municipalities throughout the country what it proposes to do to help them build new hospitals or remodel their old hospitals. We know that there is not a proper place to-day even for our returned soldiers, those who have fought in the armed forces, in the army, the navy or the air force and have returned to Canada to receive hospitalization and be taken care of, and we know that very little is being done to remedy the situation. Hospitalization and education are two of the things that should be on the priority list in our post-war reconstruction. I include education because we need new schools in many sections. Many of our schools are out-dated. We should also have up-to-date laboratories where our boys and girls can carry on research work.
In regard to hospitalization I should like to mention a case that was brought to my attention, in which the Department of Mines and Resources refused to. pay one municipality the prevailing hospital rate in that city. The prevailing rate in that city was S3 a day. The Indian Affairs branch, which comes under the Department of Mines and Resources, would pay only $2.50 a day to that hospital, which is in the red all the time since the cost is over $3 a day.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) mentioned the harnessing of power in the west, and I was pleased to hear him mention the city Df Peterborough in that

connection because our industries in Peterborough, Ontario, can supply whatever power machinery and equipment are required. We have also in the city of Peterborough an industry which wakes up every morning the workers not only in Canada but throughout the empire, for the alarm clocks made in Peterborough wake up the whole British empire.
In the speech from the throne mention is made of the fact that three new departments are being created. I would suggest that another minister be added to the cabinet, a minister of education. I believe that the people of Canada to-day would welcome a dominion educational set-up. At the present time each province has its own educational system, under which a teacher in Ontario cannot teach in Manitoba or British Columbia or a teacher in any of the other provinces teach in a different province on account of the qualifications prescribed. I would not want to see the dominion encroach upon provincial rights, but I should like to see the dominion government cooperate with the provinces in order to bring about a better educational set-up for the people of Canada as a whole. We shall never have unity in Canada unless we have proper education.
Health insurance is mentioned in the speech from the throne. Health insurance really means the minimizing of the hazards that cause sickness. When the item for industrial hygiene was brought up last year and in 1942 I suggested that every worker be examined annually, or if possible twice a year, checked for tuberculosis, and X-rayed; and I feel that if that were done we would1 have happier workers in our plants. Prevention of disease is essential also to any workable social security or health insurance set-up. We have to start at the bottom. At the present time tuberculosis is on the increase, and if that state of .affairs is allowed to develop nobody knows what will happen in a few years. In Canada the problem of sickness is not only physical but mental. Unless preventive measures are taken, in a few decades this country, instead of being the home of sound, physically fit people, will be a country of degenerates. The remedy is to start with health insurance at once, to start checking up without any more delay. I notice in the press that the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) has at last got off his hush-hush horse with regard to venereal disease. I am very glad that at last the government has come out in the open with regard to that.
I should like to know what the government is doing toward checking tuberculosis among the children of this country. I include those

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough West)
of pre-sohool age. These pre-school age children should be thoroughly checked, not once or twice but a dozen times a year, in order to prevent the child from developing, when it grows a little older, rheumatic fever, which has been the cause of so many men and boys being found unfit for service in the Canadian army.
I noticed in the Ottawa Journal of January 31 an editorial which certainly is a dandy. With the permission of the house I am going to read it:
The C.C.F., with all the courage in the world, makes no bones about v-hat are its aims. Young Mr. Jolliffe, Ontario leader of the party, is quoted in an official document as saying: "What the C.C.F. is aiming at is a system of socialized medicine as a part of a general scheme of socialization." With no worry about provincial rights, Mr. Jolliffe says: "When a C.C.F. government comes into power in the dominion (reformed health services) will be transformed with the least possible confusion and delay into a thoroughly socialized medical system which is a natural part of a socialized1 society." All the doctors young and old under the C.C.F. scheme are to be regimented and salaries and areas of work fixed, and Mr. Jolliffe says frankly that if there are any doctors who don't like it they can be left to stew in their own juice or starve.
About the C.C.F. proposals there is to be said that they are open and above board and not camouflaged by "approval in principle". Mr. Jolliffe said to a meeting of doctors in London: "The public will have to stop demanding 24-hour service; that is all there is to it." One of the doctors present asked: "Can your party arrange for all babies to be delivered between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.?" Mr. Jolliffe didn't answer that one.
Does that mean that Mr. Jolliffe spoke for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party of Canada? If so, I say there is not one of them that is 'human. And the doctors of Canada, who have done everything in the world to look after humanity here, working night and day, twenty-four hours a day, covering miles and miles and miles of rough roads, winter and summer, are invited to stew in their own juice if they do not like what the C.C.F. do! Just imagine if some hon. member happened to have an accident in his family, and when he phoned the doctor and said, "Doctor, my wife has fallen downstairs, broken her arm and, I believe, cut an artery in her head," the doctor answered "Well, I am very sorry but it is two minutes to five; I will call on you to-morrow morning after eight o'clock or after I have made out my reports in the morning."

speechtext:
I am
making the speech. And suppose the doctor went on to advise the hon. member to give his wife some sleeping tablets and maybe stick
his finger in the cut to stop the artery from bleeding! That is a lovely kind of doctrine or platform for any party to have; and God help Canada and the people of Canada if people of that kind ever get control here. But I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada to-day are awake and "wise to" these sayings of the C.C.F. party, the persons who will say something in London, Ontario, and contradict it in Vancouver; who say something in Vancouver and it is contradicted in Nova Scotia. God help the country if it should be controlled by people of that kind.
As regards health insurance, in a little booklet issued by the Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' association, entitled "Health Insurance," page 24, paragraphs 67 and 68, it has this to say:
One of the root causes of much of our ordinary sickness is bad housing, with its poor ventilation, its inadequate protection against winter cold, and its lack of sanitary conveniences. Bad housing occurs in its worst form in our city slums, -where overcrowding adds one more to the factors that breed and spread disease. Should not better housing be recognized as the joint responsibility of federal, provincial and municipal governments, and be adequately provided for in any plan of national health insurance?
That is what I said before, Mr. Speaker. We have to start at the bottom in order to build a sound basis of health insurance. We must start right in the sub-basement, so to speak, if we are to have a healthy nation.
The booklet goes on:
An important cause contributing to physical unfitness _ and the frequent spells of sickness from which many people suffer, is the made-quate income on which they have to live.
That is perfectly true. There are many people in Canada who are not receiving a proper income, and there are others who receive an adequate income but are not educated in the proper spending of that income so as to ensure good health for themselves and their families.
Poverty can be one of the worst of all disease-breeders. Its attendant evils of undernourishment and malnutrition are not only sicknesses in themselves, but they predispose their victims to every kind of infection to which they happen to be exposed. To people in that class, medical care with hospitalization can at best provide only a temporary escape from sickness, for when they are forced to go back to the old way of living, the improvement they made under medical care is quickly lost.
That again is absolutely true. I know of a young child who was taken out of a very poor home because her mother was expecting another baby. The child was taken to a certain home and looked after and given proper clothing and care, and what happened?
160	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough West)
She put on extra weight and at the end of a month was a really strong and healthy child. Then the mother wanted her back and the child returned to her old surroundings. At the end of the next month the mother came to this lady and said, "Mrs. N."-I will not mention her name-"will you please take my daughter back? She has been unwell during the past week. She has failed in health". The whole trouble was that the child did not have the proper surroundings. To continue:
The form of social security such people need most and given which they would soon have much less need for sickness insurance, is the security obtainable through steady employment at good -wages. The responsibility for providing that kind of security, based as it would have to be on national fiscal and economic policies, lies squarely at the door of the dominion government.
That does not apply merely to the workers of Canada; it applies to the farmers as well.
Now I am going to say something and I say it absolutely on my own and not for the party to which I belong. Throughout Canada during the last four or five months organizations have been issuing circulars, booklets and what-have-you, and speaking on the radio-I do not blame them for doing it-asking the people of Canada to take in all the refugees possible from Europe and to bring them to Canada. I have no objection to refugees coming to Canada, but I do say, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me, that not one refugee should come in until every man and woman, and child too-because there are some children of only fourteen or fifteen in our army-now serving in the forces are returned to civilian life and have secured jobs. I do not think these people should come in now and be given the advantage of jobs over our men who are overseas fighting for you and me, and I will fight to the last ditch the entrance of these people into Canada. I say also that immigration should be stopped until our boys and girls return from overseas and until the workers at present in our factories and war-time work return to jobs in. normal civilian life. Not until then should these refugees and immigrants be allowed into the country. I shall be criticized throughout Canada for saying this, but it is my belief, and I know there are thousands of others who feel exactly as I do. I suggest further that not one immigrant and not one refugee should be allowed in until they have had the strictest and most rigid medical examination including X-ray. And they should be examined not by one doctor but at least two, and at different examining points. We do not want these people to come into the country unless they are healthy. I would 
go further and say that those who come in should be morally and mentally well. We do not want little Hitlers in the country; we do not want screwballs-pardon the language.
In the period 1939-43, 11,510 children from babyhood to the age of seventeen were admitted to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the dinner recess I had only a few more words to say, and I believe I shall take only about five minutes to conclude my remarks. The speech from the throne contains -these words:
A broad programme has already been developed for the reestablishment of veterans of the present war, and for the care of disabled veterans and the dependents of our fighting men and merchant seamen.
I know that a great many returned men, reading that statement in the newspapers, would say it was absolutely wrong, because they feel that nothing has been done in many instances. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) also mentioned this matter this afternoon. There have been a great many men discharged from the army. In many instances they have been given a few dollars, or perhaps a small pension, but they do not want just a hand-out. These men are anxious bo be given something to do, some kind of job at which they can earn a living. They do not want to be handed a pension and told to go sit down on the curbstone and watch the parade go by. They want to be part of that parade themselves; they want to be part of this Canada; they want to help make it a great nation. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) has been very kind to me in most of the matters I have brought before him, but I feel that he should survey all the cases he has on his files, to see that these men are given not just pensions but real jobs, no matter how small. Show these men what to do, how they can make a living and become useful citizens once more. They fought for us; surely they deserve every possible consideration. I have some of these men in my own riding, and I think they are entitled to jobs after having fought for their country.
There is another matter I should like to discuss for a moment; that is, the matter of underwear for -children. At the present time many men and women are being discharged

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough West)
from our munition plants, and very little is being done to place these people in other work which will give them a decent living wage. I believe many of these men and women could be placed in the textile industry, where they might help make underwear for our children and adults. There is an absolute shortage of underwear of all kinds in this country to-day; and if God had not been very kind last fall and this winter in giving us springlike weather instead of the sub-zero weather we had last year, I feel quite sure that many children and adults would have perished from the cold. This springlike weather has also been a Godsend in that it has allowed the men in the woods to cut cordwood for next year. To return, however, to the matter of children's underwear, I know of one hospital auxiliary that has had to take sizes six, seven and eight and cut them down for babies only a year old. They have also taken worn underwear and tried to make it over for babies and young children.
I do not think the government really appreciates the need for proper underwear in this country. The men and women who work in our factories find it necessary to change their clothing very often. In Britain the women who work in the munitions plants handling explosives and powder are compelled to change their underwear at least every other day; and to make sure they do change it the government has compelled them to wear one colour on Monday and Tuesday, another colour on Wednesday and Thursday and a different colour on Friday and Saturday. I suppose what they wear on Sunday is their own business, but the government in Britain has seen that there is enough underwear to go round, and I think it is up to this government to do the same. I believe the workers who are being let out of our munitions plants should be permitted to go into the textile industry, which I think is classed as Bl.
Of course another reason for the shortage is the definite increase in the birthrate. The number of births from 1939 to 1942 was 1,001-0S2, of whom there are 936,590 now living To this number must be added the immigrant children allowed into Canada, totalling 11,510. In a letter to me under date of January 29 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated that in 1943-44 there would be 886,000 dozen garments made, as compared with 749,475 dozen in 1942-43; but many of those garments have not been made as yet, and even if they were available the increase would only give the additional children one and a half garments each.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the amendment, which states that the government has failed to lessen bureaucratic controls. The Toronto Globe and Mail of October 8, 1943, carried the following dispatch:
People who have been salvaging foodstuffs destined for destruction at the city incinerator had their knuckles rapped by the prices board here to-night.
In a statement issued on authority of the regional prices and supply representative, Stanley Lee, the board pointed out that acquisition of rationed food without surrendering valid ration coupons was illegal. A general warning was issued that unless all such articles of food were surrendered to the board, the holders would be liable to prosecution for contravening prices board regulations.
Large quantities of food, including sugar in sealed containers, tinned bacon, evaporated milk, canned fruits and jams, have been dumped at the incinerator for disposal, and some had been salvaged by nearby residents.
Well, Mr. Speaker, none of those people has died as yet, so that the food must have been good. But why should the prices board demand coupons for food that was to be destroyed? It seems to me that is carrying things a little too far. If people need the food I say, give it to them.
A short time ago I asked the Minister of Finance a question with regard to the slaughtering of cattle and other animals, and he has confirmed my understanding that the farmers of Quebec are allowed to do so, while the farmers of the other provinces are not. He went on to state that if the scheme proved successful in Quebec the other provinces would be allowed the same privilege. I feel that if the wartime prices and trade board is to function properly every province must be treated exactly the same. If it extends a privilege to Ontario then Quebec and the other provinces should have it also. If the prices board gives a privilege to British Columbia then Quebec, Ontario and all the other provinces should enjoy it also. I know of one man who has slaughtered animals for over thirty years in Ontario. He is a law-abiding citizen; yet they took away his licence and would not give it back to him, while other people are allowed to slaughter without licences. There is something wrong with the wartime prices and trade board when they play favourites like that. I believe there should be a great deal of lessening of the controls.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have used my full time.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford) : Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in the debate because I believe it is very necessary that the reactions of our people toward the

The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

speech from the throne should be made known in the house, so far as any hon. member is able to do so. I wish to join with other hon. members in congratulating the mover (Mr. Tremblay) and the seconder (Mr. Tucker) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Before I proceed further there is one matter I should like to touch upon briefly. I am sorry the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) is not in his seat because I think he should know that I consider the very thinly veiled insult which he offered in his speech yesterday to the new member from Cartier, Montreal (Mr. Rose), coming as it did from an older member of the house-or shall we say a senior member-to say the least of it was unbecoming. What did he say? Oh, he was alarmed! He was dismayed! He was horrified, in fact, that the people of Montreal, the constituency of Cartier, should have sent this new member to the house!
It seems to me that these remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, meant as an insult, will be more of a boomerang. I was not at all sorry he made them, because I think members of the house and the public generally will realize what a thin coating this "progressive" is on the Conservative party. WThen he said definitely that he was horrified at the election of this new member, what did he really intimate? What did he give out to the country at large? . His own real feelings, that he was against democracy in action, when it elected as a representative to the House of Commons a member whose views he did not happen to share. He hated to see democracy in practice. It revealed, in fact, the very core of reaction which lies within the Conservative party. In fact, he made me think he stood ' there like a very ineffective old King Canute trying to hold back the waves of progress-

speechtext:
The people of Montreal elected their member to the House of Commons because he was an honest man, because he was a man of the people, and they believe that he will represent them truly. Many of them possibly were not socialists, but they elected him for his honesty, and because they felt they could trust him. For my own part may I say this, Mr. Speaker, that I feel very 
happy to think that we shall have in this house a member who will help to do something to relieve the somewhat stuffy atmosphere of this chamber, and I am very happy to have with us a little red Rose.
After its long recess, parliament has met again in momentous times. We know that to-day the whole world stage is set for the last great act of what we hope will be the annihilation of fascism in the world, at least its heart. People the world over are ready in their places for the final conflict. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that everything which can be done by the government to add to the determination of the people, to give them courage so that they may go forward and hasten the day of unconditional surrender of the enemy, must be undertaken.
I find myself to-night more pleased to take part in this debate on. the address in reply to the speech from the throne than has been the case in previous sessions. In the speech at this session, and in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), without doubt it is easy to see the government does have a desire to participate with the other great democratic forces in the world, first, by winning the war, through a close military collaboration with the other great powers, and second, by working in the international field for sane collective measures afterwards, to try to ensure peace at least for some generations. There is the further fact that the speech from the throne did bring up, in some measure, the fact that we in Canada intend to do this in our own name; in other words, that we have achieved a degree of nationhood, something which is welcomed, I believe, both by French-and English-speaking peoples in this country.
In the months which have intervened since the house last sat vast plans have been laid for the collaboration of the democratic forces. These were made at the three important conferences of Cairo, Moscow and Teheran. The plans outlined at those conferences have given to humanity a new outlook, a new perspective, which previously we did not have. Of course we have known all along that the forces of reaction, those which have feared the progress of democracy in the world, have done everything in the past to try to divide democratic forces, both internationally and here at home. But the declarations which were made by the leaders of the three great nations at Teheran, were definitely a triumph for the democratic forces, and I believe to some degree have caused dismay among the forces of reaction. The agreements and the plans made at Teheran, while not going into intricate details which, at that time, were of course impossible, did offer a very broad scope for collaboration

The Address-Mrs. Nielsen
among the nations of the world who believe in and mean to maintain democracy. They do offer to very wide sections of the Canadian people the hope of achieving not only victory over the enemy but a peace which will give the world an opportunity deliberately to plan its future without the necessity for further war. The fact that the one great socialist nation of the world, and the leaders of the two great capitalist nations were in agreement upon these matters, gives cause for satisfaction to all of us, and does not give any of us reason to disbelieve the sincerity of those who do not happen to think just exactly the same way we do upon economic problems. I would say that, to whichever group we may belong, whether we be socialist in our thinking, or whether we still believe in the power of capitalism, very definitely we can give our support to the plans made at Teheran. The only other alternative for us at a time like this is that when the war is over we shall find, particularly in Europe, civil wars and further devastation. We shall find confusion, lack of opportunity for world trade upon which the security of our own Canadian people depends.
Therefore it seems natural and right that we should favour and do everything in our power to make concrete and to substantiate these plans, so that they may become a reality. If by any chance the plans made at Teheran cannot be carried into effect, with the world itself reverting to chaos, there is no doubt whatsoever but that the most predatory and the fiercest of the reactionary forces of the world will take the opportunity to plunge the people back into an age of servitude, another dark age, comparable with that of mediaeval-ism.
Although some of us do hope and believe that socialism will be the ultimate solution to give the fullest democracy, to give the finest well-being to our people, yet to fail to see the great step which is outlined for the whole world in these historic conferences, and not to support it would be to fail to give leadership to the people in their struggles for freedom and security and the gaining of the reforms which are definitely one step forward in the progress of humanity.
Speaking on behalf of the people in my own particular part of Saskatchewan irrespective of their party affiliations, I think I can say to you, sir, that they regard this speech from the throne as definitely an advance. The suggestion embodied in the speech that the winning of the war is our first task undoubtedly will have their support. They would urge also -and this I say to you most emphatically- that this government accept its responsibility, as one of the most important if perhaps not
loo-iii
the most important of the smaller nations of the world, in making its own definite and independent contribution to the peace plans and in establishing its own trade relationships on the basis of its own contribution in materials and men to the war effort.
Personally and on behalf of my people at home I think I can say definitely that we regret the reduction of twenty-five per cent which is contemplated in our mutual aid.
I feel that we should increase rather than decrease this contribution of money and goods.
If the long needed reforms which are promised, perhaps not very definitely, in the speech from the throne are fully implemented they will be most welcome to my people. In order to be able to make their full contribution to the winning of the war, the farmers and small town people of northwest Saskatchewan need definite assurances from this government. As the work of the house progresses I hope that legislation will be placed before us which will give satisfaction and certainty to them.
The great majority of those living in that part of Saskatchewan which I represent in this house are concerned with agriculture. Therefore their main and primary consideration is that agriculture in Canada shall rest upon a sure foundation. I think most hon. members who represent agricultural ridings will agree with me when I say that the security of agriculture depends upon the degree of world trade we are able to develop and secure for ourselves. I think rather than decreasing credits at the present time, we should be increasing them. Such action would help greatly to establish among the nations of the world which need foodstuffs a feeling of friendship which would make them willing to accept our products at a later date. I noticed the other day that one of the representatives-in the United States said this:
It is impossible for us to continue to be an island of prosperity in an ocean of adversity. We cannot be a healthy nation surrounded by a sick world.
Those words apply equally well to Canada. Upon the degree of international cooperation and trade that exist depends the security of the world in general and ourselves also. I feel that we should do more than we are' doing to advertise the products we are giving to other nations on long term credits. We should definitely develop our own policies for mutual aid to Europe and Asia to a greater extent. There was a time when we had considerable exports of grain, wheat and flour to China. In 1929 our exports of wheat and flour to China and Hong Kong amounted to
m
The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

$21,565,000. That was a considerable export, but unfortunately after 1933 it dwindled down until in 1939 we were exporting only $698,000 worth of grain and flour products to that country. There is no reason in the world why we could not regain these markets by rendering more help to China during a time of extreme need, which is right now.
I think we are in a position to tell the *people of the world that we are the producers of the finest foodstuffs to be found anywhere. We should let them know that after the war we can. supply them with agricultural machinery and all kinds of raw materials and minerals. We should advertise these things in order to make our position for export later on known to the countries of the world which are likely to take advantage of it. The well-being of agriculture in Canada depends upon our export market, but, of course, it will never be secure without the guaranteeing by parliament of a definite parity price, with guarantees to extend for a period of at least two years. That would give our farmers an opportunity to plan and regulate their production.
We welcome the suggestion of placing a floor under agricultural products, but when the actual legislation comes before the house I reserve the right to criticize it, if necessary. I hope it will not be necessary, for I definitely hope that these floors will not be basements. We do not want basements; we want the same treatment for agriculture that industry has demanded, that is cost-plus. For too long our ^farmers have been producing at less than cost and the time has come when this situation should be changed. The farming people of Canada need protection. They need a stabilization of prices by the elimination of grain gambling, and the elimination of the excess profits of those monopolies which are so closely connected with agriculture, such as the milling industry and packing plants.
I am pleased bo see that the government intends to set up an industrial development bank, but in this connection I have a suggestion to make. I would propose that in the legislation to be brought down during this session provision should be made not only for an industrial bank but for a bank for agricultural development. I appreciate that small business interests need such a bank, but I insist that even to a greater extent the smaller farmers, particularly those in the west, need a similar bank. First of all, they need a scaling down of their present debts. They need access to funds on long terms and at low rates of interest. They need the opportunity to establish themselves after the many years of drought and depression through which they have per-
(Mrs. Nielsen.]
severed and tried to keep their farms in operation. I hope the government will do what is possible to see that such a bank is instituted.
During the last recess I talked with many farming people in my province and I found that they considered it a disgrace that the province-undoubtedly because of pressure exerted by this government-is insisting upon the collection of old seed, feed and relief debts. During 1937 and 1938 there was a drought, and many of our farmers were forced to take the seed and feed which was given to them through the relief agencies maintained by this government and operated through the provinces and the municipalities. Why does this government feel that those farmers should pay back that relief? It may be said that the farmers got the relief. Certainly they got seed and feed, but when they got it they were actually producing wheat at less than cost. I do not think the Minister of Agriculture will contradict me.
