speechtext:
At some later time I shall be glad to bring before the minister definite statements from my people to substantiate what I have said.
We are very happy to think that the government will consider setting up research laboratories in western Canada, and if we have an industrial bank which will help to finance small industry, we hope that we may have set up in Saskatchewan certain industries which will improve the economy of our province and benefit our people.
No doubt many members will be speaking on the question of housing, particularly with regard to cities. But I want to assure the House that housing is not a matter of concern only to city people. Overcrowding in slum areas in the cities is a ghastly thing, but in the rural areas we also have slum conditions. There, however, it is not overcrowding but the terrible isolation which makes conditions so bad for the settlers who have to endure them. In one of the publications of the Department of Agriculture, the Economic Annalist for November, 1943, there is an article about housing conditions in Saskatchewan. It says in part:
It is readily agreed that improvements in the condition of farm homes in Saskatchewan are badly needed, and that some thought should be given towards rural housing in a broad reconstruction programme.
It goes on:
Farm houses in the pioneer fringe region are generally in poor condition. The majority of settlers' houses in this region are built of logs and are of rough construction. This situation is in direct contrast with that in the prairie and park regions where the usual house is of frame construction with a small proportion of brick and stone construction. The poorest condition of houses for the pioneer region was shown by the Goodsoil-Pierceland area.
That happens to be in the northwest comer of my riding, and in that particular area the
percentage of homes definitely acknowledged to be in poor condition was 70-2; the percentage of homes acknowledged to be in fair condition was 27-4, and those homes acknowledged to be in good condition were only 2-4 per cent of the total. So that" in our part of the country, especially if we have a development bank set-up to grant agricultural credits, we hope to see a definite and constructive programme of rural housing undertaken by the government. Not only should the government do that, but I feel that there should be some supervision over the material and equipment used and over the construction companies which undertake such a housing scheme. Unless the government exercises some supervision there will be great variations in quality and price. We need to have prices minimized and standards of material and equipment set, before a housing project of this kind can really be efficient.
We would also suggest that plans for the electrification of Saskatchewan be made at the earliest opportunity. Some of our areas on the eastern side of Saskatchewan might be linked up with the electrification which is being undertaken by the province of Manitoba. We should also do something in the development of our northern water powers. In the northern areas of my riding there are some people who live thirty miles away from the nearest telephone, and in any programme of reconstruction and rehabilitation better telephone communication should be provided for these areas. In times of sickness or accident, with people as far away from a telephone as thirty miles, it will be seen how difficult communication is, particularly at certain times of the year when the roads are impassable.
With regard to health measures, there is unanimous agreement that these are not only necessary but extremely urgent. We need these things. As far as I can gather, the great majority of Saskatchewan people are supporting the Saskatchewan state medical league. They feel that to create conditions of positive health it would not be wise or prudent to take from the incomes of those who are farming in a small way or from the low salaried workers contributions toward a national health insurance scheme. They want the best of health insurance, not a makeshift policy.
We welcome all these things, but I want it definitely known that these measures will not be an alternative to providing for the basic needs of agriculture, which are world trade and guaranteed prices. These other social security measures will just add to the security and well-being of our farming people.
The Address-Mrs. Nielsen

In the far north there are regions in my constituency where in isolated settlements only Indians and half-breeds live. I would suggest that in the period of rehabilitation, in order to give these people a little better opportunity, we might see what can be done in the matter of flooding certain areas, to give these people who live by hunting and trapping a better opportunity of catching muskrats and of selling furs. We might also consider the development of handicrafts in certain districts because that is work which Indians can very well do.
I mentioned this before but it is worth mentioning again. We would like to see an extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to include the northern areas of Saskatehe wan. In some submarginal areas people have been settled on land whioh will never be able to provide them with a decent standard of living. Some of these families might be moved, under the act, to land more suitable which would give them a better return for their labour, and the lands which they vacate could be reforested and used as game and forest reserves.
My constituency is of tremendous size, and up in the extreme northerly corner of settled territory there is an area of roughly 6,000 square miles without a railway. It is a country which is well settled. There was the beginning of a railway built there ten or twelve years ago. It was a spur line sent in from Alberta to link up with Meadow Lake and St. Walburg. That line was not completed. The roadbed ends in the wilderness. If it were completed it would give the people in that district a chance to ship their cream, eggs and other farm products. I think the building of that railway should be undertaken immediately on the cessation of the war.
I do not think the small farmers, even if we have the measures which I have advocated, will feel that they are quite secure. Therefore, on behalf of those farmers who are farming on a small scale, I think that definitely this government must guarantee to them that they have security of tenure of their land, that we make evictions and foreclosures of these small farmers impossible, because how else are these people to try to develop their farms with any degree of hope for the future? Not only that, but we should prohibit the seizure of farm machinery. Government-owned machine stations should be established, so that these people are not left to antiquated methods of old farm machinery when they can have the chance of something new and better at low rentals. Furthermore, I believe that in these areas of pioneer and homesteading the government should definitely [Mrs. Nielsen.J
decide to do something to improve the nutritional standards of the people, and by that I mean not after the war, but now. I suggest that something along the lines of the United States stamp plan should be inaugurated to enable these people whose nutrition is low and whose income is poor to have some of the grains, fruits and other surplus foods which will from time to time be available. I think the provision of school lunches for children in these pioneer areas should also be undertaken.
These are things which should not be left until after the war, but should be organized to-day, to aid and increase the ability of our farm people to put their hearts and souls into the winning of the war and to look forward with hope toward the future.
I would again recall the statement made by one of the representatives in the United States house, that it was impossible for us to continue to be an island of prosperity in an ocean of adversity. On behalf of my own people in northern Saskatchewan may I express the hope and the belief that we should never again have islands of adversity, as the northwestern corner of Saskatchewan has been in the past- islands of adversity in an otherwise prosperous world.
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency):	Mr. Speaker, I had not intended
to participate in this debate, but in view of the controversy raised by the address which Lord Halifax, British ambassador to the United States, delivered before the Toronto board of trade, on which occasion Mr. John Bracken, leader of the Progressive Conservative party of Canada was in attendance, I deem it my duty to submit to this house a few considerations which I regard as necessary.
As a matter of fact, what was stated by Lord Halifax is that, since the imperial federation exists in fact, he could not see why it could not also exist by right. I am convinced that the ambassador himself was the first to derive some amusement out of the rumpus which some people have, for electioneering purposes, raised about his address.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, from the time of the Transvaal affair to this day, have not the successive governments taken an active share in bringing about, in point of fact, the imperial federation referred to by Lord Halifax?
The Canadian government stepped in first through participation in a war whose object was to deprive of its freedom a small defenceless country which only wanted to live, Transvaal. In 1914 at the request of the British government, they once again sided with England in what was then called a "struggle for the salvation of democracy." Now, dictator-

The Address-Mr. Wilfrid LaCroix
ships have never been so numerous in Europe and everywhere else than after that war of 1914: there have been dictatorships in Germany, in Italy, in Spain, in Russia, et cetera. All of them resulted from the Versailles treaty in the drafting of which the former prime minister of Britain Lloyd George, took an outstanding part. Finally, in 1939, we declared war to guarantee the Polish boundaries, which latter, if I may say so in passing, will shrink noticeably as a result of the present conflict. Besides, here is what Lord Halifax stated on that point in the course of his address:
We can imagine the bewilderment of an intelligent visitor from another planet on being confronted with its manifest contradictions. . . . The visitor, baffled by this extraordinary confusion of functions, would suffer a further shock if he went on' to study what actually happened in September. 1939. He would find that on September 3 Great Britain declared war on Germany; that Australia and New Zealand declared war on the same day, and that South Africa and Canada followed a few days later.
He might well wonder why. He would naturally be puzzled to determine what possible interest the Polish corridor could have for a Canadian, or Danzig for an Australian, or the western frontier of Poland for a South African.
The dominions had not been parties to the Treaty of Guarantee to Poland which was the immediate cause of Great Britain's action. . . . They had influenced, but had not been responsible for, the foreign policy of Great Britain.
Lord Halifax was justified in saying, from his own standpoint: "Since you are members de facto of an imperial commonwealth, why would you not be members de jure?"
Speaking with the authority which he derived from his threefold title of Minister of Justice, right-hand man of Mr. Mackenzie King and dean of the House of Commons, when he maintained that Canada was compelled to take part in the war, Mr. Lapointe, on September 9, 1939, and February 22, 1940, uttered these words: "Neutrality is impossible." On September 9, 1939, he quoted neutrality as defined by Oppenheim "a recognized authority in international law": "Neutrality may be defined as the attitude of impartiality adopted by a third state towards belligerents and recognized by belligerents, such attitude creating rights and duties between the impartial state and the belligerents." On the strength of this rigid definition, the former minister of justice painted a dark picture of Canada remaining neutral in a war which involved Great Britain. Not only did he claim that neutrality was impossible, but he went so far as to assert that there was no such thing as mitigated, partial or sympathetic neutrality. To those who were advocating a policy of mitigated or sympathetic neutrality towards Great Britain,
Mr. Ernest Lapointe replied, on September 9, 1939, I quote:
Well, Mr. Speaker, as a constitutional student *-as I think I am

as a public man and a Minister of Justice of Canada I state, with all my responsibility, that there is no such thing as mitigated or partial neutrality.
In his recent address, Lord Halifax stated:
As opposed to that policy, which Ireland showed could be followed, the world had watched the amazing spectacle of free nations flying into common action as a result of policies in which they had had little share, but in defence of common ideals.
Ireland adds her testimony to that of Lord Halifax. On January 26, 1943, the Canadian Press released from Ottawa the following dispatch-I quote:
Mr. John D. Kearney, High Commissioner of Canada to Dublin, stated that the official attitude of the government of Eire in the present war, as defined by Prime Minister de Valera, is an attitude of benevolent and friendly neutrality. All that Ireland can do in the circumstances is to show goodwill and friendship toward the united nations. Mr. Kearney made this statement to the newspapermen to-day, on the occasion of his first visit to Ottawa, since he has assumed his post in Ireland, two years ago.
In a report on this subject, a daily French paper of Montreal stated: "Ireland's neutrality in this war is a benevolent neutrality."
Mr. Speaker, after all these gestures worthy of colonials, made by the governments which have successively held power since the Transvaal war and which the King administration has amplified during the present conflict, Lord Halifax has considered that it was only logical for him benevolently to stoop down towards Canada and charitably offer our country a seat in the imperial council that will be called, after the war, to pass on matters pertaining to the foreign policy of England.
Was it not a former prime minister of Canada, Mr. R. B. Bennett, who made the following statement, as reported by radio station CFCF, a few days ago:
I do not believe the British empire is an accident. I believe that the miracles of this war are indeed miracles, and that we have survived and will continue to do so because we have a divine mission to rule the world.
More than that, Mr. Speaker, did not the parliamentary secretary to the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, who is supposed to express the latter's views, state and define, in the course of an address recently delivered in the United States, the future policy of the Canadian government in the following terms:
Cooperation with the United States in the protection of the North American continent and
168	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Wilfrid LaCroix
of Great Britain, a country which must be considered, in these times of fast transportation, as the outpost and bastion of our continent.
Therefore, if Mr. Claxton wishes Canada, in cooperation with the United States, to contribute to the defence of Great Britain, it is because the latter is considered to be a bastion and outpost of our continent.
In a few words, Mr. Speaker, our whole war policy leans towards the views held by Lord Halifax. Is not Canada the only British commonwealth dominion without a national flag, and where the union jack is still the emblem unfurled over all public buildings? Is not our country, with its small population of some eleven million, the nation that has done most to hold that bastion, England, by a per capita war effort greater than that of any other country in the world?
Our total income, as compared with our total expenditures, have diminished from 82 per cent in 1939 to the pitifully low figure of 46 per cent in 1943. The total deficit in our budget increased from $119,000,000 in 1939 to the fantastic sum of $3,018,000,000 in 1943. The financial help granted the United Kingdom, which was not anticipated in the budget, climbed from $104,000,000 in 1939 to $1,053,000,000 in 1941, and since then, it has sky-rocketed to tremendous heights.
At the conference which took place in Toronto, Mr. John Bracken, by his presence and applause, gave full support to the words spoken by Lord Halifax. Moreover, all those who heard the speech made by the temporary leader of the Progressive-Conservative party in the house noticed that he considered the proposal of Lord Halifax, simply as a matter of controversy, when both he and Mr. Bracken should have protested and insisted that Lord Halifax leave the country never to set foot here again; for no other country in the world would have tolerated for one moment that foreign ambassador, even though a lord, ask that country to sacrifice its independence in order to please a caste of tories and imperialists who have but one thought in mind, that being to go on milking Canada indefinitely.
In the face of the unspeakable claim suggesting that we be associated to an empire with which we have nothing in common from the geographical and economic standpoints, our present-day Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) felt a sudden throb of Canadianism; this reawakening was evidenced by protests against this proposal, protests which I heartily endorse; the proposal, however, is but the corollary to an imperialistic policy for the shaping of which he must assume a large share of responsibility. We
	. IWEI
must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the audacity of the British government which, in spite of what might be said, inspired Lord Halifax, is but the natural consequence of our own weakness. Lord Halifax thought, quite simply: "If they have set the stage for this request, why should I not take advantage of it?" That is one of the reasons why, in September, 1939, I voted against Canada's participation in the war.
As far as I am concerned, I protest vigorously against the proposal of Lord Halifax, just as I have always protested, ever since I have held a seat in the house, against any tightening of the bonds which unite us to England.	.
I would much rathe'r have my country take a course leading to complete independence than follow blindly in the winding wake of England's foreign policy, a policy which will fatally lead us again into war every twenty or twenty-five years. The sooner we realize that, the better.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to state that if I disapprove of the mad effort which we are putting forth in our participation and which is out of proportion with our financial possibilities, I nevertheless wish to congratulate the government for having announced, in the speech from the throne that they intend to introduce legislation designed to afford farmers the necessary economic stability in the postwar period, through the establishment of minimum prices on the chief farm products. That is a measure which I have advocated every year since I have been a member. I am glad to note that the government has at last adopted it.
Moreover, I wish to congratulate the government for having recognized the principle of family allowances. I hope that the bill which will be introduced in this house will include no restriction as regards the number of children to whom the measure may apply. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, out of 2,486,920 families in Canada, 617,990 or 24.84 per cent live in the province of Quebec. If there are grounds for the rumour that no allowance would be granted to the seventh and subsequent children, this would deprive the province of Quebec from an advantage to which she is rightfully entitled, for it is in our province that the primary notion of patriotism which consists in giving children to the Canadian nation is best understood. Out of 84,920 Canadian families with seven, eight or nine children, Quebec accounts for 43,170, and out of the 20,890 Canadian families with ten or more children, Quebec has 13,220.
The other day I heard certain persons say that- this measure would help extend French

The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
influence in Canada. May I, Mr. Speaker, reply to this argument as follows: This legislation will tend rather to give recognition to the unsung heroism of the Canadian mother who daily in her home ignores the urge of selfishness, denies herself in order to do her humble share for a greater and finer Canada where life is worth living. In regard to the development which this legislation may give to the French tongue and influence, I assert that Canada can but benefit from two cultures developing along parallel lines without, however merging entirely. To those who out of racial fanaticism oppose the principle laid down by this legislation may I say also that no matter what may be done in regard to the use of the French language, I state positively that it will endure for, as the poet said:
Trying to stop its impetus is just like trying to prevent rosebuds from bursting into full blossom. Trying to annihilate its charm and power is like dreaming to dim the radiance of dawn.
No matter what campaigns are launched to suppress the traditions which we inherited from our ancestors, the French pioneers who settled the country, those traditions will remain alive always, for Providence willed, and rightly so, that we should stand guard faithfully, on the shores of the St. Lawrence, in this north American continent, over the genius of French thought.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the words in the speech from the throne in regard to our armed1 forces; I think they have done a magnificent job. The air force lived up to the best traditions of Canada when it took part in the battle of Britain and helped to defend that citadel of freedom in the dark days of 1940. The men of the navy have been responsible to no small degree for the winning of the battle of the Atlantic and for holding open the life-line to Great Britain and other countries. The men of the army had a tedious wait for several years, and it was remarkable that their morale held up as well as it did. However, they were ambassadors of good will in Great Britain and helped to further the splendid relationship that exists between Canada and the motherland. The women of the armed forces have done very well also. Our men are now conducting themselves wonderfully in Italy, I think far better than the general public really know. They are going through a terrible time over there, and I sometimes think the exploits of our men are taken too much for granted by the people of Canada. I believe it would be better if we knew a little more about the grim conditions under which our forces have to carry on.
That being so, let us see that when the men and women of the armed forces return to Canada they are not disillusioned by the treatment they receive. Every effort must be put forth to see that the ideals for which they fight are realized. Perhaps the majority of the workers-and I include everyone-on the home front have some realization and appreciation of the efforts put forth by our armed forces, but the more closely the hardships and sufferings of our men are brought home to the people in Canada, the more they realize the difficulties that are being encountered, the greater will be their understanding of what must be done in future for those men and women who have saved the world from nazi terrorism and brutality.
After our successes in North Africa we heard it said in many quarters that the war would probably be over by June. I never held that view, which to my mind was greatly to be deplored. Even the speech from the throne, I thought, gave that impression in the 'first few paragraphs; perhaps that impression was given because what was actually said was so overshadowed by window-dressing. Certainly it looked like a pre-election speech, and I think has been so taken by a great many people. Therefore I thought it was very timely that in his address on January 31, after reviewing the favourable position that the allies are in to-day and the position of the axis powers, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should say, as reported at page 33 of Hansard:
But I do say at once to the House of Commons and to the people of Canada that I am far from believing there is going to he an early conclusion to this war.
Something along the same line was said to the British House of Commons by Mr. Churchill. Perhaps people were beginning to think too much about the post-war period and too little about the winning of the war itself. The Prime Minister also disillusioned those who thought there would be an early general election, when he said, as reported at the same page of Hansard:
The people of Canada do not want a general election at this time of war. Our men fighting overseas do not want an election, if it can be avoided, until after victory is achieved, and we are in a position to *welcome them and all our armed forces home as a victorious army.
However, the Prime Minister left the door open pretty wide, so that I think it is obvious that in the speech from the throne he was dressing his windows and showing his wares to the people of Canada in preparation for a general election, and I imagine that if the right time should present itself the windowdressing will not count for much, though there



The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
will have to be some issue on which he will go to the country. I for one think a general election at this time would be deplorable. Look at what lies ahead of our fighting men. Perhaps we may gain some idea of the difficulties they will encounter if we look at the illustration which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star not long ago showing some of tne fortifications which will have to be overcome on the western front. Think of the terrible blood-bath that will have to be endured; think of the loss of life, the loss of property that must take place before victory is won. When we consider the care with which the campaign in Italy is being conducted it seems obvious that it will be some time before the war is over; and the war will be over only when we are in complete control of the nazi countries. Another point is that as far as I can see there is no need for a general election just now, because the government have an overwhelming majority and can do anything they like.
I have one or two suggestions to offer in connection with the reform of the procedure of the House of Commons, though perhaps some hon. members who come from a distance will not agree with them. Reform is very badly needed because of the tremendous growth of the business which must be done and the multiplicity of subjects which must be debated. I think everyone in the country deprecates the fact that to a large extent the nation is being run by order in council. I believe most of these measures should be debated on the floor of the house. For instance, order in council P.C. 9384, the wartime wages control order, was passed on December 9 only a short time before the house met. Perhaps the decision in that connection had to be made promptly; I do not know. But it seems to me that a measure of that kind might well have waited until the house was in session. Had that been the situation, some of the unrest among working men -might have been eliminated. However, so far as that measure is concerned, I know several hon. members have spoken with respect to it, and I do not wish to repeat what has been said. I simply raise my voice in vigorous protest against the measure as being un-British and undemocratic. I say it should be repealed, and we should have discussion on the floor of the house with respect to it.
It seems to me that when the committee is considering amendments to the rules of procedure some thought might be given to the length of session. We come to Ottawa in the early part of the year, remain here five or six months, and then return to our homes for the remainder of the year. Of necessity, orders in council have to be passed while we are not

here, and without debate. Why could the session not be divided into three parts, the members coming here for two or three months, and then returning home? In the first part of the session we might discuss the speech from the throne, vote moneys, pass the necessary appropriation measures, and the required supply. Then we could go away for a couple of months, and return for a further two or three months of discussion, or whatever may be necessary. We might then go away again and, if necessary, come back a little later on.
So far as I know, all orders in council of major importance dealt with by the British government are placed before parliament, and opportunity is given for their discussion when the house is in session. Under our present system I believe the government have taken advantage of the powers given under the War Measures Act to govern by orders in council to too great an extent. Also, they are unnecessarily infringing upon provincial rights. They have taken powers to which they are not entitled. As I have said before in other sessions, a great deal of discussion and many long speeches might be obviated by the introduction of a question hour. Question hours might be allowed two or three times a week during which questions could be asked, replies given and supplementary questions asked. If that were permitted I am sure much of the lengthy discussion and debate would be obviated. There is no doubt of the success of that principle in the British House of Commons.
I am. in agreement with much of the proposed legislation in the speech from the throne, but I urge that the government introduce its legislation and bring it down on the floor of the house. The people of Canada do not want window-dressing to-day. Rather, they want something concrete; promises are not enough. They want legislation.
There is a further matter I should like, on account of its urgency, to bring to the attention of the house, rather than wait until a later date. I refer to a revision of the remuneration paid to letter carriers in Toronto, a revision which is long overdue. When one compares the wages or salaries paid to other public servants, such as policemen, firemen, motormen and the like, he realizes at once that the remuneration of postmen or letter carriers which, at present, ranges from $1,020 to $1,500 a year, is inadequate. To these sums, of course, must be added the cost of living bonus.
The intelligence required to perform the arduous duties of these men is often overlooked. I have not now the time to make a comparison with other services, in figures,

The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
but the importance of letter carriers, as far as the performance of their duties is concerned, has been underestimated. The letter carrier is the last link in the system of communications. He corrects all mistakes previously made, he manipulates mail, and attends to incorrect or insufficient addressing by the public. He offers the only means of effecting delivery. He records businesses and householders, and also keeps a record of guests, home-owners, and those people who are in hospitals and hotels. All information in connection with these men is set out in a circular forwarded by the letter carriers branch No. 1-F.A.L.C. committee, which circular I have no doubt has been put into the hands of Toronto and district members. This is an urgent matter and one which should receive immediate attention. That is my reason for bringing it up at the present time.
I was pleased to see in the speech from the throne that at last the government has decided to do something in connection w-ith low-cost housing. I have discussed this matter on many occasions, and I have always been told it was one within the control of the provincial government, the cities or the municipalities directly concerned, and that it was not a matter of federal responsibility. Last year, when it was so difficult to get housing accommodation for workers in Toronto I described some of the conditions under which people were living in my own riding. In some instances I have found families with as many as five or six children living in one or two rooms. Often the house was old, in bad condition and infested with vermin, a condition which was bad for the health of the children. However, city officials did not enforce the by-laws because those people, if ejected, had no place to go. It is about time some consideration were given to conditions of that kind.
I do not wish to discuss the questions arising from the speech delivered by Lord Halifax, or from that of General Smuts. These are matters requiring careful thought ,and I do not believe we should have preliminary discussions on the floor of the House of Commons. The proper place for such discussion by the Prime Minister of Canada would be in round-table conference with the other prime ministers of other dominions. There are many intricate and complex problems involved. The Prime Minister has spoken to us about the means of communication at his hand, with which he may communicate with various members of the commonwealth, or premiers of the provinces. However, all hon. members who are in business know that in their own 100-12J
daily lives, despite the advanced methods of communication, nothing will take the place of a round-table conference. Good and all as communications are, I think we might conclude that the Prime Minister is not going to communicate by telephone with the premiers of the different provinces. I understand that they are to come to Ottawa for a conference in the near future.
It is my hope that the Prime Minister will attend the round-table conference of which mention has been made recently. I hope it will be called at as early a date as possible. Above all, I hope the Prime Minister will go over there with an open mind.
This brings me to another matter which I should like to discuss a little more fully, the question of radio. When we first set up radio in Canada an effort was made to make it a government monopoly, but times and conditions have changed. In Canada we have both free enterprise and public ownership working in cooperation with each other and the state. We have free enterprise under government control and we have public ownership under government control, both surrounded by safeguards to prevent abuse of their powers.
For instance, we have the Bell Telephone company, a free enterprise, operating in conjunction with rural telephone systems, many of which are publicly owned. We have the Canadian Pacific Railway operating in conjunction with the Canadian National Railways. We have privately owned power companies operating in conjunction with publicly owned systems; although in- different territories. All these different enterprises compete one against the other. That is a good' thing because they act as checks. But they are all operating under the control of the state. We have publicly owned water systems and some privately owned systems. At times privately owned systems have been changed to public ownership and it has been found that they did not work as successfully. We have both publicly owned and privately owned transportation systems in our cities, but they are all under control.
It is important that we should have this dual system because our whole economy has been built up on that principle. Our whole system was evolved on that principle. People talk about our democracy as being a government of the people, for the people, by the people, and let it go at that. But it is more than that. Our system of democracy is built up on one important principle, the diversification of powers of influence. Government of the people means our parliament. For the people means for all classes. By the people means that the people elect parliament. Parlia-

The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
ment is not elected by one class; it is elected by all classes. Perhaps this is done differently in other countries, but that is how it is done here. Parliament is the servant of all, of the power of capital, of labour, of the civil service, of science and so forth, and last but not least, of the power of the freedom of the individual.
Our system has been built up having in view the danger of absolute power. We have always been trying to safeguard against uncontrolled monopolistic power. This is especially bad when such power is controlled by the government or by the state. I see this as an approaching danger in connection with radio in Canada. A British statesman said, "Give me the complete use of the radio and I will elect any party to power." I think he was about :right when he said that. The absolutism of the radio corporation in Canada is becoming more intolerable all the time and is becoming more [DOT]dangerous to the country. I see great danger in the future if it is allowed to continue.
Radio in Canada is nominally controlled by the board of governors, but in fact it is not controlled by the board of governors, it is controlled by the government. At the present time it is controlled by the Liberal party. The board of governors sits every once in a while, but there are at present two vacancies on the board. In addition, there is no general manager, only an acting general manager, and there is no assistant general manager. The bylaws call for certain duties to be performed by the assistant general manager, and I do not know who is performing those duties However, enough of that. The government -runs it; so that is that. With all the excuses in the world, with all the camouflage that can be offered that it is an absolutely independent enterprise, the fact is that it just is not so.
For some time we have had the acting [DOT]general manager of the radio corporation acting as a referee as to who shall or shall not speak [DOT]over the radio, whether an address is or is not controversial, or whether it is or is not political. He decides what prominent citizens are to be given the right to speak. If the subject matter of the speech is considered to be political, then the speaker is not allowed on the radio. There have been some slight adjustments in these rules because certain parties are now allowed some time on the air.
On the other hand we hear forum discussions of the most controversial subjects and at times the discussions are inaccurate and misleading. These forums last for half an hour, and they take up subjects which could be debated for at least two or three hours before a proper conclusion could be arrived at. The inaccurate results of these things are left in the minds
IMr. Douglas G. Ross.]
of the public. Just the other day I listened to a radio broadcast over the new network coming from Philadelphia. This was a speech by a gentleman in the United States whose name l have forgotten. He was referring to Mr. Nehru of India and his persecution by the British government. I do not know anything about that, nor do I know much about Mr. Gandhi or the political significance of all this. But I do know that at the meeting of the empire parliamentary committee held here in the House of Commons the facts were given to us by members of the British government. We listened to a most instructive talk on the matter. I am not defending Gandhi or Nehru; I am simply referring to the discussion about them as an example of the controversial matters that are heard over the radio. If such things are allowed over the radio, is there any reason why other speakers should not be allowed to speak? I only make that comparsion.
Mr. Bracken was refused the use of the Radio Broadcasting Corporation facilities and there was a great deal of controversy over that decision. His speech was rejected by the referee for the corporation on the ground that it was political and that something must first be deleted from it. Who was the judge? Was it the acting general manager of the corporation? Was it the board of governors? Was it some other body that decided that Mr. Bracken should not be allowed to speak because he was too popular? But Mr. Bracken is a prominent citizen of this country and his speech was broadcast over a private radio station and also received wide publicity in the press. I defy anybody within sound of my voice to tell me that that speech was political or controversial. It was a good speech, made by a sane man on conditions in Canada and giving the speaker's suggestions as to what ought to be done. It was not a political speech in any sense, and I might add that it was very well received by the public of Canada.
Last year the committee of this house on radio broadcasting made this recommendation, at page 260 of this report:
Outstanding speakers of national importance should continue to express their views.
In view of that recommendation of a committee of this house, why was Mr. Bracken not allowed to use the national hook-up to express his views, simply because he was the leader of the Progressive Conservative party? This is not the first time that a speaker of national importance has been refused the air simply because he was the leader of a political party. But all the ministers of the cabinet can use the air all they like and their speeches are not censored.

The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)

speechtext: All right. I think it is quite proper that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should give a message to this country. But it is a different matter entirely to have political broadcasts by ministers of the crown, as has happened in the past.

speechtext: They were not very effectual though.

maintopic: QUESTION OP SUPPLY TO BRITAIN THROUGH EXPORT FROM CANADA
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If ministers of the crown are to be allowed to make political broadcasts, then prominent citizens, no matter what their political stripe, should also be allowed to give their views over the air because the public want to hear them.
The committee on radio broadcasting last year reaffirmed the principle of 1932, namely:
The paramount importance of a single national authority to control all broadcasting in the public interest.
In view of the situation as we find it and the evolution which has taken place in broadcasting, it becomes a matter of public importance that there must be set up some independent body, such as the board of transport commissioners, free entirely from the control of government, publicly owned enterprise and privately owned enterprise, which will have the authority to control radio and act impartially. This body would formulate the general principles upon which broadcasting shall be carried on in Canada so that both private and public enterprise will carry on their business according to their own policies, subject only to the control of the board. The position today is that decisions are given by an official who is under control and his decisions therefore cannot possibly be impartial. He has to make decisions, for instance, with respect to private stations and decide how much power they shall have. Imagine all that being decided by a man who is running a radio system in competition with the private stations!
A commission or board such as I have described would also coordinate all broadcasting in Canada. Another necessity for this is shown in the contradiction which appears in the recommendation of the 1943 committee on radio broadcasting. It reaffirmed the principle of the 1932 report, as follows:
The public ownership of all high-powered stations under a national system of broadcasting, with low-power stations individually operated or coordinated in relation to the dominant system.
In other words, the publicly-owned stations were to be the high-powered stations, and the privately-owned stations were to be allowed only low power.
Yet the 1943 committee recommended:
. . . that the independent stations be encouraged to improve their facilities and that they be permitted to increase their power and to arrange for multiple station hook-ups, and generally do anything that makes for better broadcasting in the public interest.
It is true that a new network has been set up utilizing the private stations, but it is under the iron fist of government control. The 1943 committee also stated:
Evidence was presented to the effect that there may be danger of losing full use of the channels now assigned to Canada by the Havana agreement.
That is so. Yesterday in the house we heard an answer given to a question put by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in respect to aviation, which is a public monopoly in this country at the present time, pointing out the strangling of civil aviation. We do not want to have our radio channels lost to us in, this country because of government radio monopoly here, but it is becoming abundantly clear that the monopoly control by the broadcasting corporation and the obstructions placed in the way of private stations has placed Canada in, a very serious position with respect to channels. We cannot be a dog in the manger. The Havana agreement definitely states that unless these channels are taken up by a certain date by Canada they may be lost to us. We have to the south of us a country of 140,000,000 people, who want to be served by radio. We already have encroachment upon our channels by the United States, and unless we do something about it we shall not be left with the channels we now have and be subject to the control of radio by the United States. There is plenty of room for competing radio chains in this country, and. for the reasons which I have stated we must not allow in Canada one all-powerful radio system.
The recommendations of the radio committee have been followed to a certain extent. Another network has been established. I do not know what the full implications of that are, but I imagine I shall find out later on.
Consider for a moment the implications in regard to other media of advertising. It is well known that paper rationing in regard toi newspapers is in effect. There are other wartime restrictions on the publishing industry which of necessity have curtailed advertising in newspapers and magazines. Direct mail and similar forms of advertising have been seriously reduced by war-time restrictions, that is by the wartime prices and trade board. These restrictions have been imposed by the government for reasons known to these industries. One of the main reasons, of course, is to curtail the demand for consumer goods and
The Address-Mr. d'Anjou

thus set up another barrier to inflation. Yet we have the spectacle of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation going into the advertising business to an increasing extent, setting up new facilities for advertising, and thereby stimulating, in this most unfair way, the demand for consumer goods, notwithstanding the edict *of the wartime prices and trade board.
Here is a statement made by the chairman of the board of governors in 1938:
Beyond the figure of $500,000 per year of commercial revenue from network and local stations, it is not desirable nor the intention of the corporation to go, and that only until we are self-supporting from other sources.
The then Minister of Transport confirmed that idea.
The latest statements of the broadcasting in 1943, given to the committee, showed that the commercial revenue was SI ,204,600. Also, the write-off from real estate, buildings, equipment, et cetera, was $411,000 on fixed assets of $800,000, or fifty per cent. Also there was a total surplus of $230,000.
Surely under present conditions there should be some reduction of the licence fee, or else the corporation does not need this commercial advertising, and it ought to be able to devote its whole time to giving good service to the public.
It is very necessary to-day, in view of the absolute powers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that another commission be appointed.
Mr. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski): (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne is interesting not so much for what it contains as to what it hints at. We are engaged in a total war and the government, in the speech from the throne, state that they intend increasing our effort if possible. However, it is the same government who told the Canadian people in the election campaign of March 1940 that our participation in the present conflict would be moderate. They have repudiated this promise together with all the others connected with our share in the bloody conflict now in progress. To ruin the country, shamelessly to sacrifice our man-power and capital, are their foremost and sole concern. All that we have is offered to the god of war, leaving nothing but ruin and bankruptcy for the Canadian people. The speech from the throne again hints at the government's intention. to authorize, in the course of the present session, the payment of another tribute of a billion dollars to Great Britain. I state right now, Mr. Speaker, that I shall oppose this measure with all my strength, as I have done on two previous occasions.
IMr. Douglas G. Ross.]
Instead of paying an annual tribute to England, the government would be far better inspired in endeavouring to relieve the distress which is to be met all over the country.
The adoption of refugees is now to the fore, as well as immigration. Ever since it has been my privilege to sit in this house I have most strenuously opposed immigration to this country. I strongly condemned the admission to Canada of immigrants picked up on the docks of London and Liverpool, and I have not changed my mind. This means, Mr. Speaker, that I am a relentless opponent of immigration of whatever kind it may be and from whichever country it may come. Let the government encourage rather than discourage large families, thus, our population will increase normally and the immigration problem will no longer exist. As regards the admission of refugees to Canada, I appose it just as strongly as I have condemned mass immigration. We did not want war and we have done nothing to foment it. Let those countries which have a share of responsibility in this war take care of the refugees whom it is proposed to pour into Canada. Let us first take care of our Canadian people, and above all let us mind our own business before meddling with the problems of others.
Mr. Speaker, I have received a large number of petitions from municipal councils in my constituency, protesting against immigration and, if one may say so, the adoption of refugees. I shall read one of these resolutions to this house:
Resolution in "opposition" to the proposed immigration of European refugees to Canada in violation of the laws of the country.
Whereas according to the Montreal Gazette, page one, the Dominion Minister of Immigration, Mr. Crerar, made the following declaration on November 3, 1943:
"Canada offers a home to refugees. An immigration agent is being sent to Europe, and the dominion.government will consider sympathetically the immigration to Canada of an unspecified number of refugees."
Whereas it is a well-known fact that the United Jewish Refugees & War Relief Agencies, with head office at 1121 St. Catherine St. West, Montreal, has circulated among the public a petition asking that Canada open her doors to all the refugees from the European continent, and that it is endeavouring, under the patronage of Senator Cairine R. Wilson, to obtain in Canada 500,000 signatures for this purpose.
Whereas in so far as such immigration will take place mostly in the province of Quebec, there is cause for alarm.
Whereas on January 7, 1944, the Canadian Press released a news item bearing the following heading:
"Canada has agreed to accept a limited number of immigrants. Refugees who come to Canada from the Spanish peninsula, according to a decision reached recently, will be given refuge for the duration of the war."

The Address-Mr. Choquette
Whereas the fact of thus allowing refugees to enter the country is not only a further encroachment upon the prerogatives of the people, but will be the cause of social disturbances now and after the war.
Whereas this question has not been submitted to the House of Commons and members of parliament should have the opportunity of voicing their views on this matter before such a policy becomes effective. It is unanimously resolved by the council of the municipality of St. Valerien of Rimouski county,
1.	That the above-mentioned municipal council is opposed to the suggested immigration plan and to any immigration on a different plan than that which has prevailed in recent years.
2.	That in any case, no amendment to existing laws and regulations governing immigration should be made unless parliament has had an opportunity of discussing the matter at the next session.
3.	That this resolution be given publicity.
4.	That copy thereof be forwarded to the Prime Minister of Canada, to the Premier of Quebec, to the Quebec provincial leader of the opposition and to the dominion and provincial members of the constituency.
Dated January 24, 1944.
(signed) Zenon St. Pierre.
mayor,
Henri Cimon,
secretary.
Seal of the municipality.
Municipality of St. Valerien.
per H. C. . . . Sec.-Treas.
Municipality of St. Valerien, Rimouski county.
I give my strongest support to resolutions passed by municipalities of my constituency opposing the admittance of refugees and immigration in general.
The speech from the throne contains the announcement concerning the adoption of family allowances by the government. I hope that this is not simply an election campaign promise but that, on the contrary, a bill will be brought down in this connection, in the course of this session. Allowances should not be granted exclusively to families of five or six children, but should apply to all families irrespective of their size.
Families of ten or twelve children are not a scarcity in the province of Quebec. Some are even larger. Personally, I am one of fifteen children, twelve boys and three girls, and I am convinced other families just as large can still be found in the constituency of Rimouski. The government, who had always refused to help large families has now an unique occasion to do so through family allowances. This is not the first time I take the opportunity of pleading this cause in the House and I shall continue to do so until the government decides to be fair to large families,
For us French Canadians, large families are our means of survival, and, as long as, in the province of Quebec, large numbers of children are brought into the world, we shall
not need refugees or immigrants from whatever country they might come; that is the way to bring happiness and prosperity to the province of Quebec and to Canada. It is all very well to say that our territory could support 200 million inhabitants, but the numeric strength of our population is less important than its quality. Even if, in ten or fifteen years from now, Canada should support only 20,000,000 inhabitants, this number of Canadian-born citizens would be preferable to 50,000,000 people drawn from every European country or, as I said before, picked up on the wharves of London or Liverpool. Personally,
I am for a Canadian population composed of our offspring, especially in the province of Quebec, of real Canadian citizens rather than of people brought from overseas and with whom attempts would be made, after the war, to merge the rest of the population of the province of Quebec. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I gladly support the petitions sent by the great majority of the municipalities of my constituency and I hope that, at least, the government will understand that helping large families-the best guarantee of prosperity for the country-is promoting their own interests.
Mr. JOSEPH-ARMAND CHOQUETTE (Stanstead) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I may say that I do not intend to trespass on the time of the house. Looking over the speech from the throne I notice that the government intends to introduce several measures of general interest. I do know, however, that if those measures were promised by a government still enjoying the confidence of the Canadian people, by a party that had shown more sympathy toward the people of this country during the last depression, I should be more hopeful of seeing those measures implemented.
That the people no longer trust the government is evidenced by the fact that in the four by-elections held in August 1943, the government candidates were defeated. The government supporters in this house were loud in their applauding the right honourable the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he spoke on January 31. They had been much less enthusiastic during the introduction of new members on January 26, the day on which parliament was prorogued, because each and every one of the new members were in the opposition.
The government now wish to redeem themselves in the public esteem, by including in the speech from the throne measures taken from the political programmes of rival parties. In September, 1943, in a speech delivered before the National Liberal Federation, a short time after the elections, the Prime Minister stated that the Bloc Populaire Cana-
The Address-Mr. Choquette

dien had but a destructive policy which raised the province of Quebec against the remainder of the country. Yet the Bloc Populaire's programme included family allowances, but the government have nevertheless discovered that the family and the home constitute the foundations of national life. They had to be reminded of that by the Bloc Populaire. With the family allowances that our political movement will ensure us, we shall have the true Christian ideal, based on fraternity and charity. Needless to say, the family is going to derive much benefit from such allowances. We all know that from 1929 to 1939 large families were those which suffered most and had to make the greater sacrifices at that time, and the governments of the time had no thought for family allowances.
Even to-day, on account of the present salary structure, the worker who has a large family, can hardly supply his children with the bare necessaries. The members of the family lack food, clothing and decent housing. The consumption of milk in the working class families is much lower than it should be, and it is the same with meat, vegetables and fruits. Too many workers live in slums. The salaries now being paid do not allow the heads of large families to give their children the bare necessaries.
In the case of the farmer, the situation is different. A farmer who has many children is unable to provide for their education and establishment. In the cities educational facilities are numerous and varied. In rural areas, when children grow up and become old enough to work, they scatter here and there. It is humanly impossible for a farmer who has many children to provide for their establishment, and frequently he must resign himself to letting them take their chance as soon as they are able to earn their living.
Such are, in brief, the difficulties which our families must face. That is why we, the supporters of the Bloc Populaire, have included family allowances in our programme. But let there be no infringement on the rights of the provinces because we hold autonomy as a sacred right. We are against centralization.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne refers to war. We are told that the German army is still quite powerful, that future operations will entail desperate fighting and heavy casualties. But are not those who plunged us into this disastrous conflict the very people who for twenty-five years have been advocating a pacifist policy? On May 24, 1938, in a remarkable speech filled with Canadian inspiration, the right honourable the present Prime Minister stated:

Our foreign and external policy is a policy of peace and friendliness, a policy of trying to look after our own interests and to understand the position of other governments with which we have dealings. It is a policy which takes account of our political connections and traditions, our geographical position, the limited members and the racial composition of our people, our stage in economic development, our own internal preoccupations and necessities-in short, a policy based on the Canadian situation.
And he added:
We have neither the power nor the will to attack any other land for our own ends. Nor are we inclined to organize or join in crusades in other continents. We have neither the power nor the knowledge to settle the destinies of countries thousands of miles away. We are no more likely of our own motion to intervene in Europe than Sweden or Bulgaria or Switzerland is to intervene in America.
Mr. Speaker, these are the very words uttered in this house barely sixteen months before our country was thrown into this war. And what have we done with this moderate, voluntary effort which had been promised? It will suffice to glance through a small pamphlet entitled Canada at War, of December 1943, to realize what the pledges of our public men are worth. Present strength of our armed forces, over 725,000 men; women in the armed forces, 37,800; in the navy, present strength 70,000 men; in the army, present strength, over 470,000 men; at present overseas, approximately a quarter of a million men; in the air force, over 200,000 men and women; maximum number of persons identified directly or indirectly with the war effort, over 1,100,000 men.
And what has this war cost us? The estimate up to March, 1944 is $10,824,000,000. And the Liberal party, and its most prominent leaders, have for the last twenty-five years promised to the Canadian people that Canada would never take part in foreign wars. The mistake made by the Conservatives has been conclusively shown, for they are responsible for the fact that 60,000 Canadians have died on foreign battlefields. And what has the first world war cost us? For the six fiscal years beginning in April, 1914 and ending in March, 1920, $1,670,406,213, including the cost of demobilization. Are we better off with the Liberals than with the Conservatives? No,, it is the same policy. For that matter, since the outbreak of the war the Conservatives in this house have supported all the important measures introduced by the government. We are sometimes told: "We must help the empire because the empire protects us." What help have we received from the empire? And we derive very little encouragement from the statement which appears on page 24 of the same pamphlet:

The Address-Mr. Choquelte
Canada at War
In 1918, after four years of war, Canada had suffered heavy losses on battlefields. So far the present conflict has not cost so many lives, hut it must be borne in mind that Mr. Churchill has declared that the 1944 campaign in Europe will be harder and more costly in human lives than all the operations carried out to date by the western powers.
And these are the consequences of an imperialistic policy, of a policy which is contrary to our interests. We are quite justified in raising a cry of alarm and in attempting a National Awakening, in order to promote the interests of Canada instead of visiting ruination upon her and jeopardizing her future. The policy of the Bloc Populaire Canadien is opposed to any effort so out of proportion to our means, and the victory in Stanstead and the success in Montreal-Cartier have shown to what extent our party meets the aspirations of the province of Quebec; however, they have given the representatives of the old parties a salutary fear.
Mr. Speaker, there is no reference in the speech from the throne to a question which cannot leave us unperturbed, the question of immigration. I have received numerous resolutions passed by the municipal councils of Stanstead county, opposing any immigration and asking
That in any case, no amendment _ to existing laws and regulations governing immigration should be made unless parliament has had an opportunity of discussing the matter at the next session.
We are opposed to any immigration until the war is over, until our armies have been demobilized and reestablished in civil life; we shall oppose any immigration until all our workers have a job enabling them to support their families decently; we shall oppose any immigration until all our workers have a healthy home; we shall oppose any immigration until our farmers are in a position to give their sons a start in life. The Government have found billions to give to England for the prosecution of the war; they will have to find money also to overcome the numerous difficulties with which we shall be faced after the war.
Mr. Speaker, has the economic crisis ended?
What legislative measures this house has passed to settle that question, I should like to know. Is it not true that the present artificial prosperity is brought about by the war and that soon, poverty will be widespread in the country, perhaps to a greater extent than even in 1939, because we are poorer and saddled with a greater debt than at that time? That is what we are attempting to avoid, Mr. Speaker.
The speech from the throne has little to say about agriculture and, at any rate, nothing very precise. It is true that for the last five years the main concern of the government has been the prosecution of the war, but has not a British minister of agriculture said that "the first line of defence of a country is agriculture"? In this country farming is the foundation, the cornerstone of the whole economic setup. What has the government done to induce farmers to produce more? Among other things, the greater part of the farm labourers have been taken for the army or sent to munition plants and the farmers are left without help after having made such tremendous sacrifices to stick to the land during the ten hard pre-war years. They are in urgent need of farm machinery, but the government request them to produce more while it is impossible for them to buy the implements and even the spare parts necessary for the operations of their farms. They have to wait long months before their orders are filled and, in spite of all that, they are requested to increase their production.
A permit is required to butcher hogs on the farm and very few farmers hold such permits. They are therefore forced to ship their hogs on the hoof on the Montreal market or others to powerful concerns who shall not be impoverished on account of the war. At these points, the hogs are kept for a number of days and their,keep is charged to the producers, because the abattoirs are short of help. Last fall, the price of pork had fallen, when the price of feed was rising. In spite of all that they are told: "You farmers are used to that kind of thing, maintain your production at the present level anyway."
This brings me to say a few words about the assistance given by the government to cooperative societies. A cooperative butter factory was refused a permit to collect the cream produced by its shareholders under the pretext that gasoline and tires were rationed. The fanners have to attend themselves to the delivery of their dairy products, which is a waste of time when the help is scarce. It is ridiculous. My hon. friend from Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), on the other hand, has pointed out the schemes worked against the Quebec United Fishermen in order to promote the interests of two large fish-dealing firms, one from Montreal and the other from Toronto. Well may we wonder whether these schemes were not intended to put the small industries, the private trader and the cooperative societies out of business.
In the economic field, the Bloc Populaire Canadien will first of all promote the maintenance and, in some cases, the reestablishment
The Address-Mr. Choquette

of private enterprise. Take good note of this: to-day anything may be done under the easy pretext that we are at war. However, even in peace time, economic .dictatorship tended to eliminate private businesses. Large trusts, powerful organizations, were crowding out the small or medium operators as well as the small and medium-sized industries and endeavouring to centralize all economic activities in the large cities. That is what we wish to avoid, Mr. Speaker. We are in favour of a new political economy to promote progress in agriculture.
Here is another article of our programme: the diversification of markets. The political value of this proposition is not so pronounced in war time; however, we expound it nevertheless as an essential element of national sovereignty. For many years past, eighty per cent of Canada's actual trade was done with two countries, Great Britain and the United States. It is easy to realize how far such a dangerous policy binds our destinies to those of the great imperialistic nations. If we ask that new markets be investigated it is not that we are opposed to those we already have, but simply that we are determined to insure that Canada will more effectively attain full autonomy.
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday, the honourable member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) suggested to the government that the representatives of the province of Quebec who are opposed to the government should be appointed to the committees charged with studying important national matters, to which the honourable member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) replied-I quote from Hansard:
The position taken by the hon. member for Gaspe illustrates what is taking place in this house with a multiplicity of parties. We do not need to tell members of this house what difficult situations arise as a result, but such is democracy and we have to meet it. At the same time a situation of this kind, which has to do with the internal economy of the house, makes it impossible to give representation, to every political party that springs up ephemerally, and temporarily I hope, in this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, who is responsible for this situation? Why have the people lost confidence in the Conservative party? Why has that party failed to name candidates in the counties of Stanstead and Cartier in August, 1943? Why is the leader of the honourable member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) outside this house? Why has the honourable member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), who was elected as a Conservative in 1940, abandoned that party sometime later, declaring that there was no room for French-Canadians in the ranks of the Conservative party? The Can-

adian people, and especially the electors from Quebec have lost confidence in the old parties who too frequently have misled or betrayed them; their policies are no longer popular, and the policy of the Bloc Populaire alone is essentially Canadian.
If I have risen in this house to take part in the debate, it was to defend the rights of the electors of my constituency who have entrusted me with a very definite mandate last summer, to demand justice for the French-Canadians of my province and to urge the adoption of a real Canadian policy. I am not here to look after the interests of Russia or England or any other country, but of Canada, my only mother country. What does it matter if mud is flung at me; for my part, I feel that my country is worth fighting for and I am quite prepared to put up with such slight inconveniences.

maintopic: QUESTION OP SUPPLY TO BRITAIN THROUGH EXPORT FROM CANADA
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make a lengthy speech, but merely to pass a few remarks. At the very outset I should like to join with the other hon. members in offering congratulations to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) and the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) upon the magnificent way in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the contents of which I am sure must have been acceptable to the great majority in this house. Never in the history of this parliament has such an elaborate programme been presented to the House of Commons for its appreciation and acceptance.
In addition to the assurance of a continued war effort, the government presents a series of social reforms which should satisfy even the most exacting, under present conditions. .First, we find a plan for social security and human welfare; second, a plan for the housing and the health of the whole population; third, social insurance against unemployment, accident, death of the breadwinner from ill health or from old age; fourth, a measure to amend and supplement housing legislation; fifth, family allowances, and sixth, a revision of the Bank Act.
These are the main points which are being brought to our attention. It is gratifying for us to note that such reforms are the work of a Liberal administration. It would be premature to try to discuss these various items at length at the present time, because the details are not known to any of us, and they will not be known until such time as the bills are placed before the house.
For that reason I shall touch upon only one point now, namely that of family allowances.

The Address-Mr. Durocher
This measure is surely worthy of our highest praise, and comes at a time when it is most needed by the Canadian people. It will help families balance their budgets, and bring up their children in a more satisfactory and appropriate manner, and at the same time it will to a certain extent relieve the wage problem in Canada. In spite of the criticism which has already appeared in some newspapers, and the remarks of hon. members, among whom were the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose), the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou) and the newly elected member for Stanstead (Mr. Choquette), I feel certain the government will see to it that this measure for family allowances covers not only so many children in a family, but all the children under a specified age. Our critics, who do not know all the facts, should wait and see what the government has to offer in this direction. We all want an increased population in this vast dominion of ours. Before we allow foreign immigration we should attempt to encourage large families and help them the best we can.
This government, I feel certain, does not wish to tell parents that if they have so many children the state will help only so many, for this would mean the establishment of a new policy of birth control in Canada, but I suggest that that has never entered the mind of any minister of the crown in the present cabinet. Birth control would be the worst thing that could happen to our society at the moment. We need more and more good Canadians. It is better to encourage large Canadian families and provide assistance from the state than to bring in foreign immigration. The latter does not always prove profitable either from the standpoint of the nation or from the assimilation with true Canadians. I have before me a clipping from La Patrie of Montreal concerning a family of seventeen children. That is the kind of family we want in Quebec. Ten of these children are below the age of fourteen. If we had more families like that our immigration problem would be solved and we would not have to touch it.
It is sometimes hard to get reforms, but a reform is needed in connection with old age pensions. Last year the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) took up this matter and drew the attention of the government to the need of raising the allowance. We were all pleased when during the last days of the session the government announced that the allowance would be raised from $20 to $25 a month. We feel that at this session the government should make an effort to increase this allowance to $30 a month and reduce the
age limit from seventy to sixty-five years. When a man or woman has reached the age of sixty-five-this applies to men more than to women-it is hard to find a new position should he or she be out of a job. No employer wants to take on anyone that old because he considers they cannot turn out the production. We should be more generous to these people. I feel certain that the government is going to look into this matter and that before the end of the session we shall have the assurance that the old age pension will be raised to $30 and the age limit lowered to sixty-five years.
I should like to refer now to the housing problem. I know there is a housing problem in every large centre in Canada, but I am better acquainted with the problem in my own city which I suppose is the same as that facing Toronto. Along with some of my colleagues this matter was taken up with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) last May, and we received the assurance that a survey would be made in Montreal and some other Canadian cities and a report submitted at the earliest possible date. Mr. Fripp of the housing administration was delegated to Montreal. I met him and went over the whole question. He spent some time in the city and then went somewhere else, and in the late fall he presented a report to the Minister of Finance. Nothing definite has come out of that, but just a few days ago I received a letter from the minister stating that the matter was receiving his earnest attention and that he hoped something definite would come out of it within the next few days. I appreciate that he has taken such an interest in this matter.
But the first of May will soon be here and, if something is not done, many people in Montreal, and I suppose also in Toronto, will be out on the street. We are looking after the older people, and we should be ready to do something for those tenants who will be without homes on the first of May. I am told that this is more a municipal problem. That may have been true before the war, but since the government can do anything under the War Measures Act I think it has now become a federal problem. Huge plants have been established in some of our cities and, while much of the population that has come in might be considered as floating population, large numbers of these people will remain. We are now faced with a position that will not improve after the war. If this is a federal problem, let us get after it without further delay. I suggested to the minister that loans bearing an interest rate of one and a half to two per cent should be made to the muni-

The Address-Mr. Durocher

cipalities. Whoever builds a home to-day must spend more money than it is really worth and, if it is built for the benefit of the state, the state should see that the man who invests his capital in a building should not be the loser in the end. There are other matters I should like to take up, but I shall wait until the appropriations are before the house. I reserve the right to discuss them at that time.
Before I close I should like to say a word about our soldiers overseas. Like many others, I have been receiving letters not only from my own but from friends and from boys of my friends. I am glad to say that each and every letter I have received seems to show that our boys are being well treated in England. They are satisfied and hope to see action at the earliest possible moment. That is the spirit we want to see in our boys. But when they come back they will expect something of us and we must have the goods to deliver. We have many social problems in hand and I realize that they represent a lot of hard work. We may not be able to do everything at once, but let us not forget that bricks and mortar are not enough to build new homes in the world of to-morrow.
